processing: Standard sheng pu-erh: pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried into maocha, then kept loose or pressed, with no ripe-style fermentation.
harvest_season: As across Xishuangbanna, spring is the prized picking and autumn the cheaper one.
appearance_dry: Typical of Mengla sheng: dark-green strands with some silvery buds, often somewhat finer than big-leaf Menghai tea.
appearance_liquor: Young tea pours a clear gold, deepening toward orange-yellow.
appearance_wet: Typically supple olive-green leaves of middling size.
taste_profile: Sellers describe a bitterness that is light, an astringency a little stronger, both clearing quickly, with honeyed floral notes and good layering.

brewing.notes: Keep the first steeps short so astringency does not take over; it clears fast, and the sweetness follows.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, like all sheng. Most of what you will find is young single-mountain tea from the spring picking, and it can be drunk now or stored. Since many old trees were lost, look for the village, such as Yanglin or Dongjiazhai, and for tree age stated plainly.
description:
Mangzhi is one of the six old tea mountains on the east bank of the Lancang in Mengla County, sitting in Xiangming between Gedeng and the rest of that old circle. It is not as famous as Yiwu or Yibang, and that is a large part of its appeal.

The tea is ordinary sheng in method, made from old trees that now stand scattered among villages instead of in continuous gardens. Yanglin and Dongjiazhai are names you will see on wrappers, and Niuguntang is the historic market village on the mountain.

What is written about the cup comes mostly from people selling it: a quick-clearing astringency, a honeyed floral scent and more layers than you first expect. Brew it short at first and let it go several rounds before judging it.

Buy with the same care as any small mountain name. Ask for the village and the year, and expect small lots.
history:
Tea gardens on Mangzhi are recorded as extensive by the Yuan dynasty. In the late Ming, merchants from central China were coming to Mansai and Sudi at the foot of the mountain to trade tea, and in the early Qing, Niuguntang was an important distribution point for the northern part of the six mountains.

The decline is told in more than one way: armed feuds in the late Xianfeng years are blamed for abandoned gardens, and another account has the mountain deserted by the late 1940s. Production picked up again in the 1980s. A legend has the name come from a place called Mang, where Zhuge Liang is said to have buried a piece of copper.
